name: Walking bass
description: steady quarters or eighths stepping and leaping through the harmony with a shape of its own: `C2q D2q E2q F2q` / `C2e G2e E2e C2e G1e B1e C2e D2e`. The default in the chorale-derived and continuo textures. It should move mostly by step with an occasional leap of a fourth or fifth to a new harmony.

name: Imitation of the right hand
description: the left hand states the subject a bar or two after the right, usually at the octave or the fifth below. This is the single most characteristic Baroque texture and it is nearly absent from generated writing. If the piece has a subject, the bass must state it.

name: Running sixteenths in one voice
description: a continuous line, the same rhythmic value throughout, changing direction and register as the harmony moves: `C2s D2s E2s F2s G2s A2s B2s C3s …`. The invention and prelude engine. Its *continuity* is the point; a rest inside it is an event.

name: Broken-chord figuration
description: `C2s G2s E3s G2s C2s G2s E3s G2s`. The C major prelude shape. Note it is written as one unbroken stream, not as bass-plus- chord: the harmony is *implied* by the figure rather than stated under it.

name: Pedal point
description: the bass holds one note, usually the dominant, for four to sixteen bars while everything above changes: `G1w` repeated, or `G1w~` tied. Bach's standard preparation for a final cadence.

name: Suspension chain in an inner voice
description: a held note becomes a dissonance when the bass moves, then falls by step, then is held again. Written with ties: `F3h~ F3q E3q`. This is where Baroque expression lives, and a texture with no suspensions sounds bland however correct the chords are.

name: Two independent voices in the left hand
description: a held tenor over a moving bass, written with `//`: `C2h G2h // E3q F3q E3q D3q`. Real three- and four-voice writing needs this; a single-stream left hand cannot do it.

name: Sequence
description: the same figure transposed down a fifth or up a fourth, two to four times. `C2e E2e G2e C3e` then `F1e A1e C2e F2e` then `B1e D2e F2e B2e`. Bach's principal method of continuation, and it should be *exact* transposition, not an approximation.

name: Alberti
description: does not exist here. It is a Classical invention. Using it makes the music mid-eighteenth-century at the earliest.

name: Chordal, all voices together
description: reserved for chorale texture and for cadential arrivals: `[C2,C3,E3,G3]q`. Four real voices moving in the same rhythm, each singable.

name: The bass rests while an inner voice takes over
description: a texture change without a change of idiom. Bach thins from four voices to two and back constantly.

name: Alberti bass
when_to_use: Simple support (stay out of melody's way)

name: Murky bass (octave alternation)
when_to_use: Simple support (stay out of melody's way)

name: Waltz bass (3/4, L:1/8)
when_to_use: Simple support (stay out of melody's way)

name: Imitation at the octave or fifth
description: a voice states the subject, another follows one or two bars later. The basic Baroque texture, and the thing most often missing from generated writing.

name: Inversion
description: the same shape upside down: every rising interval falls by the same amount. Used for the answer, for an episode, or for a later entry.

name: Augmentation and diminution
description: the subject in double or half values. Augmentation at a final entry is a standard climax device.

name: Stretto
description: entries overlapping more closely than the subject's length, so the voices pile up. Reserved for the end of a fugue; it is the intensification.

name: Countersubject
description: a fixed second line that accompanies the subject every time it appears. Invertible: it must work above *or* below.

name: Sequence
description: a one- or two-bar unit transposed exactly, three or four times, usually falling by step or by fifth. The engine of every episode.

name: Pedal point
description: the bass locks on the dominant while the upper voices work above it, for four to sixteen bars before a final cadence.

name: Voice-count change as punctuation
description: four voices thin to two for an episode and return for the next entry. This is Baroque dynamics.

name: Suspension chain
description: a held note becomes dissonant when the bass moves, falls by step, is held again. Chains of four or six are ordinary. Baroque expression lives here; a texture with no suspensions is bland however correct.

name: Circle of fifths
description: the bass falling a fifth and rising a fourth for six or eight chords. Combined with a sequence in the upper voices it will fill any episode.

name: Chromatic fourth (the lament)
description: a descending line covering a fourth by semitones: `A3 Ab3 G3 Gb3 F3 E3`. Used for grief, and often as a ground bass.

name: Compound melody
description: a single line implying two voices by alternating registers: `G3s D4s F3s D4s E3s D4s`. One hand, two audible parts. This is how a solo violin or a keyboard line implies harmony.

name: Written-out ornamentation
description: the melodic line decorated in real note values rather than with symbols, especially in slow movements.

name: Neapolitan sixth and the diminished seventh
description: at moments of intensity, usually approaching a cadence in a minor key.

name: Picardy third
description: a minor-key piece ending on a major tonic chord. The period default for a final cadence.

name: Modulation through the relative and dominant keys
description: returning through the subdominant. Bach's tonal plan is systematic, not exploratory.

name: Ritornello
description: a fixed passage returning in different keys between episodes. The concerto and many arias are built on it.

name: Binary form with a repeat
description: two halves, the first modulating to the dominant, the second returning. The dance-suite default.

name: The final entry in augmentation over a pedal
description: the standard fugal peroration: subject slowed to double values, bass locked on the dominant.

name: Written-out cadenza before the final cadence
description: a free flourish, often over a held chord, in the preludes and concertos.

name: Terraced dynamics
description: the level changes at a structural point and holds. Not hairpins, which are a later notation.

name: Steady continuo quarters
description: `D2q A2q D3q A2q`. Root and fifth alternating, one chord per bar or per half bar. The default, and it should sound unhurried.

name: Walking eighths
description: `D2e E2e F#2e G2e A2e B2e C#3e D3e`. Drives an aria or a fast movement; mostly stepwise with an occasional leap to the next harmony.

name: Repeated notes on one pitch
description: `D2e ×8`. Insistent, and used under a sequence where the harmony above is doing the moving.

name: Dotted-rhythm bass (the French overture)
description: `D2dq D2e A2dq A2e`. Stately and ceremonial. Paired with a dotted upper part; this is the single most recognisable Handel gesture and it belongs at openings.

name: Descending tetrachord / ground bass
description: `D2h C2h Bb1h A1h`, repeated as an ostinato under changing upper material. The lament bass. Handel builds whole movements on one.

name: Octave leaps between root and its octave
description: `D2q D3q D2q D3q`. Solid and plain; gives weight without motion.

name: Sustained pedal on the dominant
description: `A1w` held for four or eight bars while the upper parts intensify. Handel's standard preparation for a final cadence and for a chorus entry.

name: Sequential descent by fifths
description: the bass falling a fourth and rising a second: `D2q G1q E2q A1q F#2q B1q`. The circle-of-fifths engine, and Handel uses it plainly and often.

name: Unison with the upper parts
description: everything on the same line, in octaves, for a declamatory opening or a sudden fortissimo. Bare and public.

name: Silence under a solo entry
description: the bass drops out entirely for a phrase so a voice or a solo instrument can be heard alone, then re-enters at the cadence. Common in the arias and almost never generated.

name: Broken octaves for agitation
description: `D2e D3e D2e D3e`. The storm and rage idiom; heavier and slower than a Classical tremolo.

name: Alberti bass
when_to_use: Simple support (stay out of melody's way)

name: The French overture opening
description: dotted rhythms, slow, ceremonial, both hands in the same rhythm: `[D4,F#4,A4]dq [D4,F#4,A4]e`. Followed by a fast fugal section. The standard way to begin something important.

name: Terraced dynamics
description: `f` for a whole section, `p` for the next. No hairpins. The contrast is architectural.

name: The echo
description: a phrase repeated immediately and softer, often by a smaller group. The period's dynamic vocabulary in one gesture.

name: The grand pause before a final cadence
description: everything stops, then the cadence. Used in every chorus.

name: Homophonic declamation
description: all voices in the same rhythm on one line of text or one gesture, then back to counterpoint. Rare enough to be striking.

name: The long dominant pedal
description: eight to sixteen bars, with the upper parts accumulating. The build to a final entry.

name: Unison statement
description: everything on one line in octaves, for an opening or a sudden emphasis.

name: Sequential repetition
description: a four-bar idea stated, then a step or a third lower, then again. Handel builds by sequence more than by development, and the transposition should be exact.

name: The ground bass
description: a repeating bass pattern (often a descending tetrachord) with continuously varied material above. Whole movements are built this way.

name: Ritornello
description: a fixed instrumental passage returning between vocal or solo episodes, in different keys.

name: Da capo aria
description: A, contrasting B, then A again ornamented by the performer. If writing out the return, decorate it.

name:
The written-out cadenza before the final cadence** of an aria.

13. **Melodic sequence over a walking bass
description: the two most common ingredients, combined; it will fill any transitional passage idiomatically.

name: Wide, singable intervals
description: Handel's lines leap more than Bach's and are more vocal in shape: a rising fourth or fifth, then stepwise descent.

name: Repeated-note declamation
description: the same pitch several times in speech rhythm, for emphasis.

name: Circle of fifths
description: plain, long, and used without embarrassment.

name: Suspension chains at cadences
description: 4-3 and 7-6, the standard Baroque approach.

name:
The Neapolitan sixth** at a moment of pathos in a minor-key aria.

19. **Picardy third** to end a minor-key movement.

20. **Slow harmonic rhythm
description: one chord per bar or per two bars, especially in the grand choruses. Handel prolongs where Bach moves.

name: Deceptive cadence to extend a close
description: V to vi, then the cadence restated and completed.

name: Walking quarters through the harmony
description: `D3q A2q Bb2q F2q G2q D2q Eb2q A2q`. Steady, mostly by step or by fourth, one note per chord. The default and the sound of the style.

name: Circle of fifths, exact
description: the bass falling a fifth and rising a fourth, four to eight chords in a row: `D3q G2q C3q F2q Bb2q E2q A2q D2q`. Corelli uses longer circles than anyone before him, and the exactness is the point.

name: Suspension chain (the 7-6 or 4-3 chain)
description: the upper voices suspend in alternation while the bass walks down by step. `D3q C3q Bb2q A2q` under suspending violins. This is the single most Corellian texture there is.

name: Pedal on the dominant
description: `A2w` held for four to eight bars before a final cadence, with the violins intensifying above.

name: Repeated notes for insistence
description: `D3e ×8` under a sequential passage.

name: Bass imitating the violins
description: in the fugal movements the bass takes the subject at the octave below. The trio sonata's fast movements are usually fugal and the bass must participate.

name: Descending tetrachord ground
description: `D3h C3h Bb2h A2h`, repeated. Used for the slow movements and the chaconne-like finales.

name: Long notes under a solo passage
description: whole notes while a violin ornaments freely above. The slow-movement texture.

name: Cadential 4-3 with the bass falling a fifth
description: `A2h D2h` under a suspended fourth resolving. Every phrase ends this way; that is not monotony, it is the period's punctuation.

name: Sequences of one-bar units
description: the same bar transposed down a step or a third, three or four times. Corelli's principal method of continuation, and the transposition should be exact.

name: Silence for one beat before a cadence
description: the whole texture stops, then the cadence lands. Sparing and effective.

name: The suspension chain
description: the two violins suspending in alternation while the bass walks down by step, 7-6 or 4-3, for four to eight bars. The single most Corellian texture, and the sound the whole style is remembered for.

name: Imitation between the two violins
description: one states, the other answers a bar later at the unison or the octave. Constant in the fast movements.

name: Voice crossing between the violins
description: the second rising above the first for a bar or two. Gives the trio texture its interweaving quality.

name: Fugal exposition in a fast movement
description: subject in violin 1, answer in violin 2, then the bass. The church sonata's second movement.

name: Parallel thirds and sixths between the violins
description: for a lyrical passage or the approach to a cadence.

name: Circle of fifths
description: longer than anyone before him, six or eight chords, with a sequence in the upper parts. His signature progression.

name: The 4-3 cadence
description: the upper voice suspends a fourth over the bass's penultimate note and resolves down to the third. Every phrase ends this way, and that consistency is the period's punctuation, not monotony.

name: The Corelli clash
description: the resolution of a suspension sounding briefly against the note it resolves to, in another voice. Named after him.

name: Secondary dominants inside a sequence
description: each step of a circle tonicised. Systematic rather than expressive.

name:
The pedal on the dominant** before a final cadence, four to eight bars.

11. **Picardy third** to end a minor-key movement.

12. **Even harmonic rhythm
description: one chord per beat or per bar, held for a whole section. Irregular harmonic rhythm sounds later than this style.

name: Exact sequence
description: a one- or two-bar unit transposed without variation, three or four times, usually falling by step or by fifth. Do not vary it; the exactness is the idiom.

name: Slow–fast–slow–fast
description: the church sonata's four movements: suspensions over a walking bass, fugal, a shorter slow movement often in the relative key, and a dance-like finale in triple time.

name: The dance suite alternative
description: allemande, corrente, sarabande, giga, each in binary form with repeats.

name: Ground bass
description: a descending tetrachord repeated with varied upper material, for a slow movement or a chaconne finale.

name: Ritornello contrast in the concerto grosso
description: the full group (*concerto grosso*) answering the soloists (*concertino*), with the same material.

name: Regular four- and eight-bar phrases
description: Corelli is squarer than almost anyone, and the regularity is the frame the suspensions hang on.

name: The written skeleton, performer-ornamented
description: slow movement lines are intentionally plain and were decorated in performance. If writing the ornamentation out, use passing notes, cadential trills and turns around long notes.

name: The cadential trill
description: on the penultimate note of every significant cadence, resolving to the final.

name: Terraced echo
description: a phrase repeated softer. The whole dynamic vocabulary.
